issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not coherent with the stated trauma type. For a relief worker in a war zone, family-related comments could plausibly be relevant, but crash imagery specifically centered on cars hit by accident points toward a road-traffic trauma rather than war-zone relief exposure. The trigger profile therefore mixes two distinct trauma contexts without supporting items linking them.

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies only partially fit the trigger/appraisal pattern. Avoiding social contacts can follow family-related shame or guilt, and avoiding authority figures can fit war-zone exposure, but the set does not clearly connect to the unusual crash-imagery trigger. This makes the coping profile look like it is addressing a different trauma configuration than the trigger items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: Negative appraisals of intrinsic fault and failed role are plausible for a relief worker, but in combination with the crash-accident trigger they create a mismatched formulation: the appraisals imply guilt/responsibility and role failure in humanitarian work, whereas the trigger item implies a motor-vehicle accident trauma. These elements are hard to reconcile as one coherent trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger profile is not well aligned with the trauma type. For a relief worker in a war zone, police and generic surveillance could be plausible, but recurrent 'cars hit by accident' imagery points toward a road traffic accident trauma rather than war-zone exposure, and no other items anchor this to the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: Avoiding authority figures or uniforms is only weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The trigger item specifies police rather than military, aid command, or armed personnel, making this strategy feel trauma-mismatched for a war-zone relief worker unless other items supported detention, abuse by authorities, or checkpoint-related threat, which they do not.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'There is something about me that made the event happen' is not impossible, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the other selected items. 'Failed Role' fits a relief-worker trauma well, but a strongly self-causal intrinsic blame statement is less coherent without memory or threat content suggesting a specific preventable mistake or personal causation. This creates a mild but meaningful formulation mismatch with the otherwise role-failure/ongoing-reactivity pattern.

vignette:
A year ago, Leo had been a relief worker in a conflict zone, distributing food and medical supplies in a small town that was overrun by militia forces. He remembered the day clearly: the sudden crack of gunfire, the chaos of people running, and then the moment he found himself pinned behind a collapsed wall, a soldier in a dark uniform standing over him, shouting orders he couldn't understand. Leo had frozen, his hands empty, his supplies scattered in the mud. He had been certain he was going to die, and in that instant, he felt a profound failure-he was supposed to be helping, not cowering. That sense of helplessness had never left him. Now, back in his university town, he was a student again, but the world felt fundamentally different. He had come to believe that his body had betrayed him; it kept reacting as if he were still in that alley, his heart hammering at the slightest unexpected sound, his muscles tensing for a threat that never came. He was convinced that he had failed in his most important role-to protect and serve those who needed him-and that this failure was a permanent stain on who he was.

The triggers were everywhere, and Leo found himself unable to escape them. When he walked to campus, he would see a police car parked at an intersection, and his stomach would drop. The sight of a uniform-whether a campus security guard or a delivery driver in a military-style jacket-made his breath catch. He felt watched, as if eyes were on him from every window and every passing car, and he was certain that at any moment, someone in authority would turn on him. These moments of intense fear, which came several times a day, only reinforced his belief that he was still in danger, that his body was right to be afraid, and that he could not stop bad things from happening. The more he felt watched, the more he was convinced that the world was a place where he was powerless and at fault.

In response to these triggers, Leo had developed a set of strategies that he knew were shrinking his life. He avoided making eye contact with anyone on the street, keeping his gaze fixed on the pavement to avoid the feeling of being observed. He stopped going to the student union or the library, places where he might see people he had socialized with before his deployment, because the idea of small talk felt impossible-how could he pretend to be normal when he was so broken inside? He also began taking long detours to avoid any street where he might see a police officer or a person in uniform, and he would cross the road if he saw someone carrying a backpack that could contain a weapon. These avoidances had become a daily ritual, a set of rules he followed to keep the fear at bay. But the rules themselves were exhausting. He had stopped responding to messages from his old friends, and his coursework was slipping; he was no longer attending lectures because the walk to the building required passing a campus security booth. He told himself that if he just avoided these things, he could keep the panic from overwhelming him, but the avoidance only confirmed his belief that he was not safe, and that he was weak for not being able to handle it.

The cycle had tightened over the months. A single trigger-the sight of a uniform-would send him into a spiral of negative appraisals. He would think, I failed. I couldn't protect anyone. I can't even protect myself now. These thoughts made him feel more watched, more vulnerable, as if the world itself was confirming his worst fears. He would then avoid eye contact with the next person he saw, which made him feel even more isolated and convinced that everyone could see his shame. He had come to believe that his body was his enemy, that the racing heart and sweating palms were proof that he was still in that alley, still helpless. What frightened him most was the thought that this would never end-that he would always be this afraid, always this alone. Last week, after a student in a security uniform walked past his apartment window, Leo spent three hours unable to move from his chair, his mind replaying the soldier's face. It was then that he finally called the university counseling center, hoping, though not believing, that someone could help him stop the loop.
